title: Why Does Your Voice Go DEEP With Fingers in Your Ears? 👂
description:
Try it: stick your fingers in your ears and talk. Your voice goes deep. That's your skull singing bass: every word you say makes your bones hum, and that low hum normally leaks out of your open ear canals. Plug them and it's trapped, so it booms straight into your eardrum (audiologists call it the occlusion effect: the lows, under about 1,000 Hz, can get up to about 20 decibels louder). Same reason your voice sounds boomy with earbuds in, and the same skull sound a recording of you never hears. Press harder and there's a faint rumble on top: the muscles holding your fingers in, buzzing about 25 times a second (first heard this way in 1810, measured at 25 Hz in 1980). Did your voice go deeper? Yes or no?
